profile.name: Quentin F. Davis
profile.tagline: I build gameplay systems, AI companions, and production software, then draw the worlds they live in.
about: I am a software engineer who works in C++ first and has spent the last several years building things that have to run, not just demo. Two of my systems are deployed and in daily use: SyncBridge, an Azure-backed orchestration service that keeps five meeting and recording platforms in sync, and WorkingDoc Automation, a FastAPI app that imports, merges, and reconciles authorization records without destroying the manual corrections people have already made.

The other half of my work is real-time. Project Hunter is an Unreal Engine 5 action RPG built on the Gameplay Ability System, where character capability lives in components rather than one enormous pawn so combat, stats, and traversal can be iterated separately. REVIA is a local-first desktop AI companion I originally prototyped in Python and then rewrote in C++ with Qt 6, running llama.cpp and whisper.cpp on the user's own hardware with SQLite-backed memory. Rewriting it taught me more about latency, threading, and lifetime management than any tutorial project would have.

I have also been drawing for seventeen years, which is not a side note. Character sheets, background paintings, and colour work are how I learned composition, readability, and what a player's eye actually does with a frame. It is the reason I care about UI hierarchy in UMG and Qt as much as I care about the systems underneath, and why I am most useful on teams where gameplay code and presentation are not separate conversations.

detail.overview: Project Hunter is a long-running Unreal Engine 5 prototype exploring how far modular, component-driven architecture can carry an action RPG. Survival horror pacing sets the tone: movement costs something, resources run out, and enemy pressure is meant to be read rather than out-clicked.

projects.heroAlt: REVIA desktop assistant interface with profile and voice settings
projects.imageAlt: REVIA desktop assistant interface with profile and voice settings
projects.summary: A local-first Windows companion written in C++ and Qt 6, with persistent memory, mood tracking, speech, and screen awareness, all running on the user's own hardware.
projects.details: Originally prototyped in Python, then rewritten in C++ for latency and control. Work is routed through Reflex, Fast, Main, and Expert lanes across differently-sized local models while the assistant still presents as one identity.
highlights: Rewritten from Python into C++ and Qt 6
Local inference through llama.cpp and whisper.cpp
SQLite-backed persistent memory and mood tracking
Sandboxed filesystem and bounded UI automation

detail.overview: R.E.V.I.A (Reactive Emotional Virtual Interactive Assistant) runs entirely on local hardware. Conversation, memory, mood, speech, and vision all stay on the machine. It began as a Python prototype with a PySide6 controller; the current build is a C++ and Qt 6.8.3 rewrite, undertaken to get latency, threading, and object lifetime under real control rather than fighting an interpreter.

sections.title: Architecture
sections.body: Work is routed through specialised lanes - Reflex, Fast, Main, and Expert - backed by several GGUF-quantised models of different sizes. The lanes share one identity and one memory store, so the specialisation is invisible from the outside: there is only ever one Revia. Built with CMake and Ninja, targeting Windows 10 1809 and later.

sections.title: Local Model Stack
sections.body: Nothing leaves the machine unless the user asks it to.
items: Conversation through local Qwen models on llama.cpp
Speech recognition via Distil-Whisper on whisper.cpp
Local text-to-speech synthesis
Persistent memory in SQLite

sections.title: System Awareness and Limits
sections.body: The assistant can act on the machine, but every capability is deliberately bounded.
items: Ambient screen awareness across multiple monitors
Sandboxed filesystem operations
Bounded Windows UI Automation tasks
Opt-in internet research through a visible, restricted browser

sections.title: Why the Rewrite
sections.body: The Python build proved the product; the C++ build is about making it responsive and consistent enough to leave running all day. It is an active personal project, prioritised toward a stable personality rather than a finished consumer release.

implemented: Local conversation, speech recognition, and TTS
SQLite persistent memory and mood tracking
inProgress: Lane routing across Reflex, Fast, Main, and Expert models

sections.title: What Was Built
sections.body: Everything in the proof of concept was made solo: the scene and dialogue systems, the branching conversation flow, the levels, and all of the character art.

sections.title: Why It Stopped
sections.body: Scope outgrew what one person could finish alongside other work. It stays in the portfolio because the proof of concept is real, complete, and still running - and because the character work from it is some of the art I am happiest with.

projects.name: Portfolio Showcase
projects.subtitle: This site: a data-driven showcase engine with no framework
projects.heroAlt: Portfolio home page showing the layered hero and the four discipline gateways
projects.imageAlt: Portfolio home page showing the layered hero and the four discipline gateways
projects.summary: The site you are reading. A layered, selection-driven showcase built on native ES modules with no framework, where every project's presentation is described by data rather than special-cased in code.
projects.details: One rendering engine drives both the project and art showcases. Atmosphere, hero artwork, and layout are all resolved from fields in a single JSON file that is schema-validated in CI.
highlights: No framework and no runtime dependencies
Data-driven presentation, no per-project code
Schema-validated content with unit tests
WCAG AA contrast and reduced-motion support

detail.overview: Rather than a page of cards, this portfolio is a showcase: selecting a project re-composes an entire scene - atmospheric background, large foreground artwork, information, and selection UI - with a crossfade between selections. It is built on native ES modules with no framework and no runtime dependencies.

sections.title: Data-Driven Presentation
sections.body: The rendering engine contains no knowledge of any individual project. A project declares a theme, a hero image, a hero style, and optional detail content, and the shared showcase decides how to present it. Character renders are drawn as free-standing cutouts; screenshots are presented in a floating window frame. Adding a project never requires touching the renderer.

sections.title: Architecture
sections.body: Responsibilities are split into focused modules rather than one large script.
items: Showcase engine: selection state, filtering, and transitions
Ambient background: layered scene, framing, and motion
Asset resolution, theming, and shared UI fragments
Media viewer and details drawer overlays

sections.title: Content and Quality
sections.body: All content lives in one JSON file validated against a JSON Schema, with unit tests covering category handling, URL safety, theme resolution, and deep links. Colour contrast meets WCAG AA and all motion respects prefers-reduced-motion.

implemented: Responsive desktop, tablet, and mobile compositions
